title: Human-AI dialogues can reduce feelings of partisan animosity
description: Affective polarization – and especially dislike of opposing partisans – is a source of major concern. Consequently, there is great interest in identifying effective approaches for depolarization. Here, we ask whether recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), namely the development of conversational large language models, can be leveraged to reduce affective polarization. Prior work suggests that such AI-powered chatbots can be powerful tools for changing factual beliefs. However, it remains unclear whether dialogues with an AI chatbot can reduce feelings of animosity towards members of one’s political outgroup. To answer this question, we assign N = 3,874 US-based participants to one of three treatments in which an AI chatbot tries to reduce affective polarization, to a control where they have an irrelevant dialogue with the AI, or to a benchmark condition consisting of the top-performing non-AI intervention identified in a recent mega-study. We find that all of the human-AI dialogue treatments significantly reduce animosity towards opposing partisans and discomfort with having opposing partisans as neighbors or close friends, with the most effective AI treatment achieving treatment effects roughly 70% the size of the effect of the top-performing non-AI intervention benchmark. In addition, we find that the human-AI dialogues increase the likelihood that individuals reciprocate social ties with hypothetical social media profiles associated with their political outgroup by approximately five percentage points, performing at least as well as the non-AI intervention benchmark. We find that supplying the AI chatbot with specific facts about the outgroup increases effectiveness. These findings indicate that providing factual information is an important route to depolarization, and that AI chatbots offer an effective approach for reducing affective polarization that has the potential to be deployed at scale online.

title: Young children use mental simulation to reason about their performance
description: Young children can use observed performance outcomes (e.g., successes and failures) to decide when to persist and which tasks to pursue. However, learners often face situations where outcomes either cannot be observed or are uninformative. Using a simple tablet game, we asked whether preschool-aged children can use mentally simulated outcomes to guide their decisions. In Experiment 1, the game froze mid-trial so the final outcome was unavailable. Children preferred to repeat the same game when their attempt would have resulted in success (versus failure). In Experiment 2, an on-screen agent intervened mid-trial, rendering the outcome uninformative about the child's performance. Children preferred to play the game without (versus with) the agent when their attempts would have been successful without the agent's intervention. These findings suggest that children can simulate alternative outcomes of their actions and use them to guide how they pursue future tasks.

title: Temporal Convolutional Network Modeling of Eye Gaze Reveals Gaze-Based Implementation Strategies in Proactive Cognitive Control
description: Proactive cognitive control involves the sustained maintenance of goal-related information to guide behavior in anticipation of upcoming processing demands. Using predefined areas of interest (AOIs), Reimer et al. (2025) demonstrated that gaze behavior during the cue–probe delay of the AX-Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT) can index individual differences in proactive control. However, analyses of gaze data based on predefined AOIs may collapse across distinct gaze-based implementation strategies. The present study used an unsupervised sequence-modeling approach to examine dynamic gaze-based implementation of proactive control during the cue–probe delay of a spatially modified AX-CPT (Reimer et al., 2025). A Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), trained without access to cue identity or behavioral outcomes, extracted latent representations of trial-level gaze trajectories that were clustered into four distinct gaze states. These states reflected sustained cue-directed gaze, cue-congruent anticipatory orienting, cue-incongruent anticipatory orienting, and spatially diffuse rightward orienting. Critically, cluster prevalence predicted individual differences in proactive control (PBI), dissociating effective from ineffective forms of anticipatory implementation and indicating that these gaze patterns do not simply reflect task structure but instead index qualitatively distinct control states with different behavioral consequences. Together, these findings demonstrate that unsupervised temporal modeling can recover interpretable, behaviorally meaningful gaze-based strategies, showing that proactive control varies not only in degree but also in implementation quality.

title: Global environmental ideologies cluster into four distinct cognitive archetypes
description: Standardized assessments of environmental attitudes typically assume a universal psychological structure, where populations differ in the degree of concern but not in the organization of beliefs. Here we challenge this assumption by applying network analysis to data from 35,617 individuals across 28 countries and regions. We show that global environmental ideologies do not follow a singular logic but cluster into four distinct topological archetypes. The Western Core cluster (including the USA, Australia, and most Western European nations) exhibits a polarized structure organized around environmental skepticism, where environmental protection is positioned against economic priorities. The East Asian cluster (Mainland China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan) displays a network with weak conditional associations despite high edge density, suggesting that environmental attitudes are shaped more by social norms than by internal cognitive consistency. The Transitional Economy cluster (Hungary, Russia, Thailand, and South Africa) is characterized by a moderately dense network centered on environmental skepticism, forming a coherent belief package. Finally, the Global South cluster (India and the Philippines) shows the sparsest network structure, dominated by a strong link between perceived helplessness and low environmental priority. These results demonstrate that low psychometric consistency in non-Western contexts often reflects meaningful structural adaptation rather than measurement error. We conclude that effective climate communication depends on leveraging these diverse cognitive architectures rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all Western model.

title: Examining predictors of adaptation to a non-uniform formant perturbation and the construct validity of assays of sensory acuity
description:
Purpose: Interindividual differences in the magnitude of adaptation to non-uniform formant perturbations have been consistently observed, yet individual characteristics that can account for these differences remain poorly understood. Here, we assess whether the sensory acuity and production variability measures that were proposed to predict adaptation to simple, uniform perturbations also predict adaptation to complex, non-uniform ones. We additionally assess the construct validity of these auditory and somatosensory acuity measures. 
Method: 78 participants completed a battery of assessments of auditory acuity, somatosensory acuity of the tongue, and vowel production variability. Subsequently, participants produced words containing the four American English corner vowels while exposed to a non-uniform centralization perturbation pushing vowel formants towards the center of the vowel space. Adaptation was measured globally as changes in vowel spacing (the average distance between each vowel pair) and for each vowel individually.
Results: Average vowel formant variability was the only significant predictor of overall adaptation, with less variable participants adapting more. This finding partially aligned with vowel-specific results, where variability predicted adaptive changes for /u/ but not other vowels. None of the sensory acuity measures predicted adaptation either overall or for any individual vowel. Auditory acuity was moderately correlated across the four corner vowels and for pure tones; somatosensory acuity was not correlated across tasks. Higher auditory acuity predicted lower production variability overall, but not for any individual vowel.
Conclusion: Our results, though mixed, suggest that individual characteristics in production ability better predict adaptation to a non-uniform formant perturbation task than sensory acuity, contrary to previous findings for uniform perturbations which have mainly found a relationship between adaptation and auditory ac

title: “It’s Ok—Not Everyone Has to Be an Einstein”: How Unequal Treatment in the Classroom Gets into Children’s Heads
description: Achievement inequality is a pressing societal problem: Children from low socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds underperform in school, even when they have the same ability as their high-SES peers. Why? In this article, we offer one piece of the puzzle by showing that children face unequal treatment in the classroom. The unequal treatment may be driven, in part, by a seemingly benign stereotype that portrays children from low-SES backgrounds as “strivers” or “go-getters” rather than naturally gifted. As a result of this stereotype, teachers may offer children from low-SES backgrounds inflated praise when they succeed, unsolicited help when they struggle, and pity when they fail. Such practices, although well-intentioned, may convey to children that they lack ability and are unable to cultivate their ability, which undermines their motivation and achievement. To counter these dynamics, interventions should target the pervasive societal beliefs—such as the belief in meritocracy—that sustain them.

title: The Impact of Screen Time and Social Media Use on Adolescent Wellbeing: An Instrumental Variable Analysis
description: Amid worsening mental health of adolescents, the proliferation of digital technologies over the last two decades has attracted particular attention as one potential contributing factor. However, there is a widely cited lack of causal evidence and most prior studies rely on correlational designs vulnerable to reverse causation, unmeasured confounding, and measurement error, while being limited in geographic scope. We estimate the effects of screen time and social media use on adolescent wellbeing using data from 615,133 fifteen-year-olds across 54 countries, applying instrumental variable methods that exploit cross-national and temporal variation in digital environments during the rapid technological diffusion of the mid-2010s. We use year-specific country-level Information and Communication Technology (ICT) usage index and social media penetration rate as instruments generating exogenous variation in adolescents' digital engagement. Instrumental Variables analyses indicate that higher screen time and more social media use caused lower wellbeing in the mid 2010s. The findings were robust to assumption testing and robustness checks. This study contributes multinational causally informed evidence to an empirically contested but policy-relevant debate on the impacts of digital technology on adolescent wellbeing.

title: Developing the Playground Heroes program: An evidence- and theory-based approach to promote positive bystander behavior in racist bullying
description:
Background: Racist bullying is a serious societal issue that can have detrimental effects on the health and development of victimized children. To address racist bullying, we developed the Playground Heroes program, aimed at promoting positive bystander behavior targeting pupils and teachers. This article describes the systematic development of this theory and evidence based program. 
Methods: The Playground Heroes program is based on the GATE-BULL intervention and developed using the Intervention Mapping approach. A need assessment was conducted based on relevant literature, focus group discussions with pupils and interviews with teachers to gain more insight into factors that influence bystander behavior. The results led to the development of a program consisting of a lesson plan with a serious game and classroom activities, a teacher training, and a parent brochure. Prior to the start of the lesson plan teachers complete the teacher training about racism and addressing racist bullying. The lesson plan starts with the serious game which is followed by classroom activities matching the scenarios of the game. Primary schools are recruited by cold calling and through online flyers. The evaluation plan concerns a non-randomized controlled trial, consisting of an intervention group and a control group, with one measurement at baseline, and two follow-up measurements at four and eight weeks. 
Discussion: Using the Intervention Mapping approach resulted into the systematic development of a theory and evidence based school program to promote positive bystander behavior in racist bullying.

title: Babble and First Word Learning: The Articulatory Filter Revisited
description: Production and perception of speech develop in tandem during the first year of life, shaping one another in ways that have only recently been put to the experimental test. Canonical babbling, which emerges robustly between 6 and 8 months across languages, is grounded in neuromotor maturation but also depends critically on audition. To account for how production experience might shape word learning, Vihman (1993) proposed an ‘articulatory filter’ that spotlights adult speech patterns matching an infant’s emerging motor routines. Here we trace this proposal to its origins and review the experimental evidence from the past 15 years, much of it using Vocal Motor Schemes (VMS) – frequent, stable consonantal patterns identified from naturalistic recordings – as an index of phonetic mastery. Studies employing VMS demonstrate that infants’ production patterns modulate their attention to and memory for both nonwords and familiar words, and that earlier VMS attainment predicts later lexical and phonological outcomes. Recent acoustic work has begun to validate the VMS construct, while parallel lines of research extend the logic to the pre-canonical period and to infants’ attraction to the sound of infant voices, especially their own. With further validation, VMS may serve as an early clinical indicator of vocabulary delay.

title: Taxing working memory shifts the balance from goals to stimulus-response habits
description: Despite our familiarity with the concept of habits, eliciting and measuring habitual “slips of action” experimentally in humans has proven to be difficult. A possible explanation is that participants in psychological experiments actively recruit goal-directed control and therefore make few habitual slips-of-action in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes. In the current experiment we used the symmetrical outcome-revaluation task in combination with a working memory load in an attempt to tip the balance from goal-directed control to stimulus-response habit. During the instrumental learning phase, participants learned to make a Go response to stimuli signalling valuable outcomes (and points) while not responding (NoGo) to stimuli signalling not-valuable outcomes. During the subsequent test phase, the outcomes signalled by the stimuli were either value-congruent with training (still-valuable and still-not-valuable), or value-incongruent (devalued and upvalued). Participants had to flexibly adjust their behaviour on value-incongruent trials where the stimulus-response association learned during training was no longer appropriate. For half the participants, a concurrent working memory load was imposed during the test phase. In line with our preregistered hypotheses, participants showed evidence for habitual slips of action across two experiments, but those under working memory load showed increased habit tendencies (specifically failures to inhibit prepotent Go responses in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes). This central finding suggests that a working memory load can be used to reveal habits in humans.

title: Task-Related Interference During Educational Activities: A Meta-Analysis of Its Occurrence and Relationship with Learning
description: While learning, students experience various kinds of thoughts. Some of these thoughts are fully on the task, but others might be about aspects of their private life or how they can apply what they are currently learning. These thoughts that are not fully on the task can be divided into task-unrelated thoughts (TUTs, also known as mind wandering) and task-related interference. Task-unrelated thoughts are independent of the task, while task-related interference thoughts may bear some relationship to the specific learning task. Prior research has largely focused on how often task-unrelated thoughts occur and how they relate to learning outcomes. There is a paucity of research on task-related interference leaving a gap in understanding of the prevalence of these thoughts and their influence on learning outcomes. This meta-analysis aimed to determine the frequency of task-related interference (TRI) and its correlation with learning outcomes. Results show that TRI occurs 20.54% of the time, yet no significant correlation with learning was observed. These findings suggest TRI should be accounted for alongside mind wandering, as the available evidence does not support a systematic relationship between TRI and learning performance, unlike for TUTs.

title: Age Differences in Flexibly Binding Memory of What, When and Where
description: Experiences are multimodal and often involve what, when and where aspects. Past research in young adults has shown that a core function of memory is to learn flexible associative structures connecting all three aspects. We investigated how normal cognitive aging affects multimodal memory associations and retrieval flexibility of partial or complete events. In two experiments, 63 younger (18–35 years) and 50 older adults (65–85) completed a spatio temporal object memory task in which they encoded object sequences appearing at different screen locations over repeated exposures, and then retrieved either object-only, location-only, or complete object-location sequences. In both age groups, memory for object sequences was best, followed by location sequences and object-location combinations, with older adults showing a disproportionately amplified pattern. Cross dimensional analyses showed that for both age-groups object-only sequence retrieval partially relied on location knowledge, and vice versa, suggesting that both age-groups used multimodal binding to scaffold sequence memory. Younger adults showed greater flexibility in modulating binding strength depending on retrieval demands, compared to older adults. Computational modeling revealed that a two-system model, assuming parallel learning of within-dimension transitions and cross-dimensional binding associations, adequately captured participants’ performance. Younger adults relied more on binding associations than transition learning, while older adults showed more balanced reliance. Our results indicate that reductions in binding flexibility contribute to adult age differences in remembering sequentially structured experiences.

title: The Influence of Lifestyle Activities on Midlife Memory Performance
description: A wealth of evidence supports the positive influence of physical, cognitive and social lifestyle activities on cognitive aging. However, the specific contributions of these lifestyle domains to memory performance in midlife, and the role of dementia risk, remain underexplored. This study investigated how self-reported lifestyle engagement during youth (13-30 years) and midlife (30-65 years) was associated with long-term memory performance in 399 middle-aged adults (mean age = 51.89 years). Participants completed a continuous report episodic memory task which measured both retrieval success (accessibility of memories) and memory precision (accuracy of fine-grained details). Lifestyle engagement was assessed using the Lifetime of Experiences Questionnaire (LEQ) and dementia risk was classified based on family history. Memory precision showed a significant negative association with age and was lower in participants with family history of dementia. In contrast, retrieval success was significantly associated with lifestyle engagement during midlife. When examined by lifestyle type, social engagement during youth and cognitive activity during midlife were both positively associated with retrieval success. These findings indicate that at midlife, memory performance is already being differentially influenced by specific types of lifestyle engagement that has occurred throughout the lifespan. The results also suggest a distinction in the factors influencing memory retrieval success and precision. Specifically, lifestyle engagement was more closely linked to memory accessibility, while biological factors including age and family history of dementia appeared to influence memory precision. This distinction offers new insights into the mechanisms through which lifestyle may support memory across the lifespan.

title: Meta-Awareness of Mind Wandering: Examining Effects of Self-Regulated Learning, Interpolated Testing, and Self-Explanation
description:
Background
Mind wandering is a common experience for students that negatively impacts learning outcomes. Research has attempted to mitigate the impact by including interpolated testing in the context of learning from videos. The results of these studies are mixed and indicate that interpolated testing may not have a practical effect on reducing mind wandering.
Objectives
In the present study, we aim to investigate whether writing self-explanations has a stronger effect than interpolated testing on reducing mind wandering and improving learning outcomes. We al-so explore whether self-regulated learning skills are related to meta-awareness of mind wander-ing.
Methods
138 participants were recruited across three groups and presented with the same video to review. The first group was the control group. The participants in the second group answered interpolated tests, and the third group wrote self-explanations at pauses in the video. All participants complet-ed a knowledge test before and after watching the video to compare group learning outcomes. Additionally, participants completed questionnaires measuring their self-regulated learning. Self-caught thought reports were used in anticipation that participants expecting to write self-explanations would engage in metacognitive monitoring and thus become meta-aware.
Results and Conclusions
We found no significant difference between the groups regarding knowledge gain or meta-awareness. Interestingly, higher scores on metacognition and online task strategies subscales of self-regulated learning were associated with fewer thought reports. However, the number of thought reports written correlated positively with knowledge gain, indicating that meta-aware learners perform better on subsequent knowledge tests.

title: DyscalcBattery: An open browser-based psychophysical battery for dyscalculia screening and numerosity perception research
description:
We present DyscalcBattery, an open-source, browser-based psychophys-
ical battery for assessing the cognitive substrates of developmental dyscal-
culia. The tool implements seven established paradigms — Simple Reac-
tion Time, Dot Enumeration, Symbolic Number Comparison, and four non-
symbolic comparison tasks (dots, objects, shapes, and colour-diversity) — in
a single self-contained HTML file deployable on any laptop or tablet running a
modern browser. Unlike existing dyscalculia screeners, which are proprietary
and Western-norm calibrated, DyscalcBattery is permissively licensed,
requires no installation, runs offline after first load, and is designed for low-
resource and multilingual field deployment. The battery exports trial-level
CSV data including reaction times, accuracy, Weber-fraction estimates, and
subitizing slopes, and ships with R analysis scripts for downstream psycho-
metric fitting.

title: “Do as I Say, Not as I Do” - The role of hypocrisy metaperceptions in conversations about pro-environmental change
description: Pro-environmental change necessitates discussions about the environment, yet many people avoid such conversations. We propose that this reluctance may partly stem from hypocrisy metaperceptions: because environmental issues are inherently moral and discrepancies between concern and action are common, advocating for behavioral change without acting accordingly may be associated with concerns about being perceived as hypocritical. We investigated whether inducing feelings of hypocrisy reduces willingness to talk about environmental solutions, and whether this differs for individual-level versus system-level change. In a multinational online experiment (N = 957) across six European countries, participants were randomly assigned to a hypocrisy induction or control condition and reported their willingness to discuss individual- and system-level environmental solutions, as well as their metaperceptions of appearing hypocritical. While the hypocrisy induction did not significantly affect metaperceptions or willingness to talk, structural equation modeling revealed a negative association between hypocrisy metaperceptions and willingness to discuss both individual- and system-level change. Our findings suggest that the anticipated social costs of appearing hypocritical may contribute to the silence surrounding environmental discourse, potentially undermining the very conversations needed to drive both individual behavior change and system-level change on environmental issues.

title: Can personality be deliberately changed? Effects of a randomized, placebo-controlled intervention on character strengths and Big Five personality traits
description: The promise of intentional change in adult personality traits attracts broad interest, even as convincing evidence remains scarce and methodologically challenging. In a preregistered randomized placebo- and waitlist-controlled study with N = 3,434 adults, we tested whether an eight-week online training of a self-selected character strength produces short- and long-term changes in character strengths (states and traits) and Big Five personality traits. Participants in the intervention condition increased targeted strengths states more than both placebo and waitlist control conditions. However, intervention and placebo participants experienced similar gains in targeted strengths traits, extraversion, and agreeableness, as well as similar decreases in neuroticism relative to the waitlist condition. Thus, some effects may result from non-specific aspects of the structured activity. Informants did not observe any between-condition differences in strengths trait change. These findings underscore the importance of using rigorous control conditions in research on volitional personality change.

title: Cognitive Abilities, Personality, and Sustainable Attitudes and Behavior
description:
Climate change demands urgent action, yet individual engagement in sustainable
behaviors remains inconsistent. To better understand the factors that promote sustainable
behaviors, we conducted two studies (N₁ = 280, N₂ = 973) examining how political
orientation, personality traits, reasoning ability, social-emotional-behavioral skills, and
complex problem solving relate to sustainable attitudes and behaviors in U.S. adults. Using
structural equation modeling, we found that openness to experience was the strongest
predictor, alongside liberal political orientation and self-perceived social engagement and
innovation skills. Unexpectedly, both reasoning ability and complex problem solving showed
consistent negative associations with sustainability outcomes, challenging assumptions that
cognitive abilities universally facilitate adaptive behavior. Psychological characteristics
together explained approximately one-third of variance in both sustainable attitudes and
behaviors. Personality traits dominated explanation of attitudes, while behaviors emerged
from more balanced contributions across psychological domains, with social-emotional skills
providing meaningful incremental validity beyond established predictors. These findings
demonstrate that personality psychology provides crucial insights for understanding
environmental engagement, revealing that adaptive social-emotional competencies and
personality characteristics are more strongly associated with sustainability than cognitive
abilities.

title: Ancient Influencers: The role of prestige bias in the appreciation of annotated historical text documents
description:
Historical manuscripts are appreciated for their intellectual content and cultural importance, but their aesthetic and cognitive impacts, particularly for copies that contain post-production annotations, have received relatively little attention. Drawing on prestige bias theory, we tested whether author/annotator reputation and annotation relevance shape contemporary aesthetic engagement. The study employed a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial designs to orthogonally manipulate Author reputation (famous vs. non-famous), Annotator reputation (famous vs. non-famous) and type of Annotation (relevant vs. non-relevant). We used eight historical text documents, each with eight different preambles rotated through the design scheme via Latin Square. On each trial, participants (N = 430) first read the preamble (one of eight different conditions), then viewed the manuscript page at their own pace, and finally provided 7-point Likert ratings on 13 different aesthetic-affective evaluation dimensions. Results showed that participants looked longer at manuscripts labelled as being authored and annotated by famous people, compared to conditions where either the author or the annotator were less famous. Condensing the ratings into five orthogonal factors (Aesthetic Appeal, Gravitas, Positive Connection, Orderliness, and Negativity) revealed that relevant annotations were associated with higher Gravitas scores than non-relevant annotations. Additionally, the factor Positive Connection scored higher for famous authors, famous annotators, and relevant annotations. Our findings demonstrate that reputation (for both author and annotator) and annotation relevance shape contemporary responses to pre-modern manuscripts. These findings advance prestige bias theory in aesthetic domains and offer practical implications for museum curation and manuscript scholarship.

Keywords: Historical text; Annotation; Reading culture; Cognitive Psychology; Prestige

title: Using large language models to track national identities
description: National identity drives a range of political action, from civic engagement to intergroup violence. We present a novel and accessible approach using large language models (LLMs) to label texts for expressions of positive (national identification, patriotism) and defensive (nationalism, national narcissism) national identities. We test four popular LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Llama 4 Maverick) across 13 million words sourced from social media, surveys, and political speeches in 25 languages. Our findings reveal that LLMs label texts reliably and in a theoretically-consistent manner, producing judgments that closely match those of domain experts and outperform both dictionary-based approaches and crowdworkers—also reducing the cost by a factor of 1,000 compared to the latter. An analysis of US presidential addresses using the best-performing LLM (GPT-4o) reveals that expressions of national identities have doubled over the twentieth century. Further studies revealed differences between Republicans and Democrats. Defensive national identities were five times more prevalent in Republicans' social media posts than in Democrats'. Such identities were also frequent in the speeches of populist leaders around the globe. Together, these findings demonstrate that LLMs offer a reliable, valid, accessible, and cost-effective approach to labeling texts for nuanced expressions of national identity, enabling new insights into its role in contemporary and historical social trends.

title: Simpler, but Not for All: Unequal Gains from Text Simplification
description:
Background: Text simplification is a strategy for improving the accessibility of institutional communication. It is assumed to function as benefiting all readers, including those with low literacy skills. However, empirical evidence on its effectiveness across different proficiency levels remains scarce and mixed.
Objective: This study investigates whether meaning-preserving text simplification improves comprehension and processing efficiency for readers with low and typical levels of proficiency, and whether its effects are moderated by cognitive and experiential factors.
Methods: Nine pairs of texts were presented in standard and simplified versions. Typical Readers (TR) and Low Readers (LR) completed reading tasks followed by comprehension questions and subjective evaluations. Linear mixed-effects models were used to analyze the effects of text version and group. Moderation analyses were conducted using components of the Simple View of Reading and print exposure.
Results: Simplification increased reading speed, but not reading comprehension. While TR outperformed LR across tasks, there was no interaction between text version and group. Only a modest improvement in comprehension measure emerged for TR in planned contrasts. Subjectively, TR showed trend-level sensitivity to simplification, whereas LR did not differentiate between versions. Moderation analyses suggested that simplifications helped individuals with higher cognitive skills and greater print exposure. 
Conclusions: The findings challenge the assumption that text simplification functions as a universal accessibility tool. The pattern of results suggested limited and selective advantages that were more apparent among readers with greater literacy-related resources.

title: No evidence for the age-based imitation bias in a culturally diverse sample
description: Humans possess learning biases that guide them to imitate individuals likely to hold adaptive information. One proposed bias—the age-based imitation bias—suggests that children preferentially imitate adults over peers because adults are presumed to have greater instrumental and conventional competence. Although supported by studies with young children from the post-industrialized west, this bias has not been examined across broader developmental ranges or diverse cultural contexts. Therefore, here we investigated adult versus peer imitation in 369 children aged 3–17 years from four communities: Congolese BaYaka, Congolese Bandongo, Scots, and Chinese Americans. Across instrumental and conventional tasks, we found no evidence that children preferentially imitated adults over peers. These null findings may reflect an existing publication bias in the social learning literature. They also raise the possibility that reported age-based effects may have been activated by the presence of other state- and model-based biases embedded within previous experiments.

title: Short dialogues with AI reduce belief in antisemitic conspiracy theories
description: Antisemitic conspiracy theories have been central to anti-Jewish prejudice for centuries. Given their longevity and deep ties to religious, ethnic, and ideological identities, debunking them presents a particularly difficult challenge. Here, we test whether having believers discuss their chosen antisemitic conspiracy with a large language model (LLM) prompted to debunk such conspiracies can reduce belief and improve attitudes toward Jews. In a preregistered experiment (N = 1,224 U.S. adults endorsing an antisemitic conspiracy theory), participants were randomized to a dialogue with an LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) prompted to debunk their belief, or one of two control conditions. The debunking dialogue substantially reduced belief in antisemitic conspiracies relative to controls overall, and increased favorability toward Jews among those participants who were initially unfavorable. These findings show that even deeply rooted, identity-linked conspiracies can be effectively debunked through factual correction, offering new insight into prejudice reduction and suggesting that LLM chatbots may offer a route to reducing antisemitism at scale.

title: Beyond Trait Scores: A Framework for Contextual, Role-Specific Behavioural Assessment in High-Stakes People Decisions
description: High-stakes people decisions now extend beyond hiring to promotion, redeployment, retention, and workforce restructuring, often under time pressure and growing governance scrutiny. Traditional psychometric instruments have made important contributions by standardising evidence about individual differences, but they were not primarily designed to produce role-specific, evidence-cited behavioural reasoning for live organisational decisions. This paper proposes the Contextual Behavioural Assessment Framework (CBAF), a conceptual and methodological framework that shifts the unit of analysis from trait description to situational behavioural inference. The framework integrates four design principles: career-stage calibration, role and environment contextualisation, scenario-based behavioural elicitation grounded in situational judgement test methodology, and cross-dimensional AI-supported inference. The paper reviews literature on personnel selection, situational judgement testing, trait psychometrics, AI in HR, algorithmic fairness, explainability, and auditability. It also distinguishes practice-informed conceptual development from formal empirical validation. The CBAF is presented as a responsible assessment architecture for making behavioural reasoning more relevant, transparent, consistent, and auditable while preserving human authority at the decision layer.

title: M^3: Meta-cognition and Meta-control with Markov Decision Processes
description: Intelligent behaviour requires monitoring and adjusting ongoing cognitive processes to the changing demands and constraints of internal and external environments. This is studied in terms of  meta-cognition, cognitive control and meta-reasoning, and, recently, as the expected value of control and the value of computation. However, integrated consideration of core problems such as state representation, generalization, and prospective versus retrospective calculations of the long-run value of meta-computational policies is lacking. We offer a recursive partially observable Markov decision process framework in which meta-cognition is a form of meta-level perception, and, just as for control itself, meta-control algorithms can be fractionated into costly but adaptive model-based, or fast model-free strategies.  Understanding how the brain implements self-adjustment has both clinical and engineering significance.

title: Consensus-based Checklist for Assessing Scientific Objectivity
description: Objectivity is widely regarded as crucial for scientific practice, yet it remains poorly understood in scientific methodology and, as a result, has limited impact on research practices. Building on recent developments in the philosophy of science, we have created a new methodological tool, an easy to use checklist, for assessing the objectivity of scientific practice reported in academic publications or grant proposals. Developed through an expert-consensus study, this checklist can be used both to retrospectively evaluate objectivity of completed research and to prospectively guide the design of future experiments.

title: Minds Meet Machines: Trust and Intellectual Humility as Necessary Conditions for AI Persuasion
description: Recently, AI models demonstrated a remarkable ability to facilitate opinion change, a notoriously difficult task between human communicators. Here, we focus on the dispositions that characterize message recipients, specifically identifying trust in AI, intellectual humility (IH), and their interplay as key factors in acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Across two studies with an online British sample (N=294), we replicated findings showing significant attitude change regarding legal immigrants following brief interactions with GPT. Crucially, our findings reveal that opinion change is contingent on higher IH and greater trust in AI, independently and jointly, predicting greater acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Experimentally capturing the centrality of open-mindedness (IH) and source sensitivity (Trust) highlights how epistemic vigilance constrains AI’s persuasive impact and sheds new light on the persuasion literature by revisiting the role of source credibility. Future research should examine whether these dispositional effects extend to long-term behavioral patterns across broader real-world contexts.

title: Unreported use of artificial intelligence in three ABAI publications:  A call for more transparency
description: In the past three years, large language models have been transforming how behavioral scientists conduct research. One area in which these models may prove useful involves academic writing. Although journals recommend reporting the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic writing, the extent to which researchers adhere to these guidelines remains an open question. To examine this issue, we extracted a total of 381 articles published in 2022 and 2025 in Perspectives on Behavior Science, Behavior Analysis in Practice, and The Psychological Record. Then, each article was submitted to two AI-generated text detectors to determine whether it was written by a human or AI. The detectors identified 14 articles that met the threshold for being at least partly written by AI, but only one reported its use. Furthermore, approximately 25% of articles published in 2025 produced scores significantly different from the distribution of scores from articles published in 2022. Unclear reporting guidelines may explain part of these results. Hence, we recommend that journals update their guidelines to encourage the reporting of any use of AI in academic research, including editing, rephrasing, translating and writing.

title: Balancing Competing Goals when Coordinating over Rule Construction
description: Even competitive activities require cooperation to agree on the rules. How do people navigate this tension, and what conditions help them reach agreement? We study rule negotiation in a collaborative game design task (N = 184) where dyads propose and vote on what game to play, crossing two factors: communication (chat available vs.~vote-only) and role uncertainty (whether players know which role they will occupy). We find communication increased agreement rates and role uncertainty had only a minimal impact on agreement. When players knew their role, they proposed games that subtly favored themselves, balancing self-interest against the need for acceptance. Chat content was largely coordinative rather than argumentative: players declared preferences and deferred rather than playing hardball. Our findings highlight how deliberation helps people coordinate on rules, even when they know which side they're on.

title: Interval scales in the wild: A large-scale evaluation of the viability of Rasch models for producing interval scales
description: It is widely recognized that common analyses of test and survey data assume that score scales have interval, not just ordinal, metric properties. Although this assumption cannot be directly falsified in most contexts, it is falsifiable when the claim of an interval scale rests on the application of the Rasch model to responses to binary items. This is based on falsification tests enabled by Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis of the adherence of response data to axioms of additive conjoint measurement. Recent work has proposed a bootstrapping method for improving the interpretability of results by creating a basis for falsification of the claim that the Rasch model, fit to a given dataset, has produced an interval scale. With such a procedure available, we now ask: how frequently, if ever, do psychometric data appear to produce an interval scale under the Rasch model? In this study, we apply this bootstrapping procedure to 86 datasets of binary item responses found in the Item Response Warehouse. Claims that the Rasch model is a superior measurement model to other Item Response Theory models or that the scale resulting from fitting the model to one’s data has special status rely on the notion that the Rasch model can produce fundamental (i.e., interval-scaled) measures where other models cannot, due to its alignment with the principles of conjoint measurement. Our study begins to shed a wider light on the extent to which this promise is ever realized in practice, which appears to be rare and to occur in settings where one would not expect Rasch measurement to be successful.

title: Tracking the Erosion of Democratic Norms: Panel Evidence Spanning the 2024 US Presidential Election
description: Most citizens of democracies express commitment to democratic norms that preclude behaviors such as pardoning political allies and ignoring judicial rulings. But what happens when leaders at the highest level engage in such behaviors? Do people stand firm and condemn such behaviors regardless of party? Or do their commitments to democratic norms weaken? This study provides the first multi-wave panel evidence tracking U.S. citizens’ reactions to concrete, real-world episodes of elites violating democratic norms. Prior to the 2024 US Presidential election, we identified 15 specific potential violations of democratic norms. In a six-wave survey from October 2024 through June 2025, we tracked Republicans’ and Democrats’ attitudes towards violations of each of these norms, triggering new survey waves as Presidents Biden and Trump committed potential norm violations. We find evidence that support for democratic norms substantially weakens after a co-partisan president commits an apparent democratic norm violation. Conversely, support for democratic norms is either unaffected or strengthened after an out-party president’s apparent norm violation. Approximately 50% of partisans became more permissive of their own party’s violations, and a similar share became less permissive of out-partisan violations. Together, these responses capture an erosion of democratic norms marked by growing inter- and intra-party polarization.

title: A Reversal of Visual and Semantic Dominance in Scene Representations from Perception and Short-Term Memory to Long-Term Memory
description: Scene images encapsulate complex information, integrating both perceptual features and semantic meaning. It is therefore difficult to disentangle their unique contributions in scene mental representations. Moreover, the relative contributions of visual and semantic information may vary across different cognitive systems. To quantify the unique contributions of visual and semantic information to scene representations, we leveraged visual and language deep learning models, to capture pure visual information from scene images and pure semantic information of the textual descriptions of their categories, respectively. Using representational similarity analysis, we measured the unique variance these visual and semantic models explain in the representational geometry of visual scene representations across perception, short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM).  We found that scene representations were visually dominated in perception, while they were semantically dominated in LTM. The relative contributions of visual and semantic information to the representations in STM were similar to perception but differed from LTM. Using the same approach, we replicated the visual dominance in perception and STM in participants’ drawings of scene images. Taken together, these findings reveal a reversal of visual and semantic dominance between perception and LTM and demonstrate that visual working memory maintains primarily visual codes. This framework offers a powerful new way to separate and quantify visual and semantic contributions, which are typically intermixed in human mental representations, advancing our understanding on how visual knowledge is represented across different cognitive systems in the mind and brain.

title: Mesmer’s error: Beliefs reverse the rubber hand illusion (a Registered Report)
description: In the rubber hand illusion (RHI), participants report ownership of a fake hand which is stroked in synchrony with their own concealed hand, with lower ownership ratings for asynchronous stroking. This effect has been historically attributed to multisensory integration. However, such a pattern of results is consistent with experimental demand characteristics, and an alternative theory proposes that the RHI is an effect of phenomenological control (PC; the trait ability to change experience to satisfy goals). To date, support for a PC theory of the RHI has been limited to correlational evidence. Here we conduct a pre-registered causal test of the relative contribution of these two proposed mechanisms in RHI effects. 25 high PC participants (top 15%) were tested in an RHI procedure and the classic effects of greater response for synchrony than asynchrony were replicated. The procedure was then repeated following imaginative suggestions for a reversal of the classic effect (i.e. greater synchrony than asynchrony effects). Ratings of ownership and proprioceptive drift were modulated by suggestion. Effects for ownership and drift were reversed. Exploratory analysis showed the same pattern of results for referred touch ratings. Participant beliefs arising from demand characteristics dominate over multisensory mechanisms in RHI ownership of a fake hand and proprioceptive drift. Multisensory synchrony is neither necessary nor sufficient for the rubber hand illusion. Claims of an illusion beyond that attributable to demand characteristics and phenomenological control require experimental evidence from controlled experiments

title: A Computational Theory of Dignity
description: People seem to hold a variety of conflicting intuitions about the concept of dignity. Here, we seek to reverse-engineer the computational basis of these intuitions. We propose a Bayesian model that casts intuitions about dignity as computations about what agents' actions imply about their own and others' social rank. We show through two behavioral experiments that our model captures people's intuitions well, reconciling seemingly conflicting intuitions with a common computational framework.

title: A luminance-induced expansion aftereffect
description: We report a novel luminance-induced expansion aftereffect in which adaptation to sawtooth luminance modulation with a slow decreasing phase causes subsequently viewed static patterns to appear to expand. Eight observers were adapted to luminance ramps and judged the appearance of subsequent static and contracting test patterns. The magnitude of this expansion aftereffect was quantified using a nulling paradigm; the illusory expansion was cancelled when the test pattern contracted at ~ 0.3°/s. This expansion aftereffect is qualitatively distinct from the brightening aftereffect previously associated with sawtooth luminance adaptation, suggesting dissociable perceptual consequences of luminance-change adaptation for brightness and spatial coding.

title: Why Intentions Fail to Become Action: A Threshold Account of Action Initiation
description: People often intend to act, recognize why the action matters, and still do not begin. This article argues that such failures reveal an under-specified transition in psychological theories of behavior: the moment at which intended action becomes capable of onset. Existing theories explain central parts of the action sequence, including intention formation, implementation planning, self-regulation, effort allocation, and habit. Yet behavioral onset is often treated as a downstream consequence of these processes rather than as a transition with its own enabling conditions. This article develops a threshold account of action initiation. On this account, intention can orient the person toward action, but onset occurs only when effective activation exceeds a resistance- and state-sensitive boundary. Initiation, therefore, depends not only on wanting or planning an action but also on readiness, execution compatibility, attentional stabilization, initiation resistance, structured instability, and prior trajectory. Integrating evidence from intention-behavior research, implementation intentions, procrastination, educational delay, health behavior, digital engagement, and within-person variability, the article distinguishes intention from action possibility and onset from persistence. The account generates falsifiable predictions concerning conditional intention effects, nonlinear onset, resistance manipulation, execution compatibility, path dependence, and structured variability. Its contribution is to specify when valued and intended actions become capable of beginning.

title: Value-based decision-making and behavioural economic constructs that distinguish people with and without cannabis use history
description: Behavioural economic accounts posit distorted valuation processes underlie cannabis decisions; however, less is known about the moment-to-moment dynamics through which value influences observable choice behaviour. This study explored whether value-based decision-making and behavioural economic constructs distinguish people with and without cannabis use history. Sixty participants were recruited, half with history of cannabis use (cannabis group), and half without (control group). Participants completed a value-based decision-making task (choosing between previously rated cannabis-related and cannabis-unrelated images). A drift-diffusion model was fitted to behavioural data (choice and response time patterns) to estimate reinforcer-specific parameters, including evidence accumulation rates and response thresholds. Compared to controls, participants with cannabis use history had higher cannabis evidence accumulation rates (p = .023). Exploratory analyses revealed higher self-report cannabis demand across most indices (all except Pmax; ps ≤ .042). However, groups did not differ in cannabis-unrelated evidence accumulation rates or response thresholds for either decision type (ps ≥ .186). Notably, controls showed higher cannabis-unrelated than cannabis evidence accumulation rates (p = .001). People with a history of cannabis use ascribe a higher value to cannabis than those without such history, who in turn value cannabis less than alternative reinforcers—a pattern consistent with behavioural economic accounts of addiction.

title: Pole-Augmented Multidimensional Scaling Framework for Survival-Analysis Visualization
description:
We introduce a multidimensional scaling framework that represents survival
outcomes and covariates in a single two-dimensional map. Two reference points called poles
represent the event direction and survival or non-event direction at a fixed follow-up time.
The poles and covariates are represented in a multidimensional scaling space, such that each
covariate is closer to one pole. This representation is intended to combine two readings in a
unified visualization, namely, the relational structure between covariates and each covariate
location relative to the two survival-outcome poles. The event pole is built from the martingale
residual of a null Cox model, while the non-event pole is built from a Kaplan–Meier
pseudo-survival quantity. To produce a clearly interpretable unified visualization, Pearson
correlations between items are converted into distances using three category-specific exponents
for the pairs of covariate–covariate, covariate–pole, and pole–pole. The proposed
framework is evaluated on the Rossi recidivism dataset (N = 432). Financial aid and marital
status are closer to the non-recidivism pole, while prior convictions and race are closer to the
recidivism pole. A simulation under Cox proportional hazards provides a known coefficient
structure, with positive- and negative-coefficient covariates near the event and non-event
poles, respectively.

title: Hunger and Concentration in Daily Life: Inter-Individual Differences and Breakfast-Related Variation but No Robust Average Association
description: Momentary reductions in concentration may affect daily functioning. In addition to external distractors, bodily signals might divert attention from ongoing tasks. Hunger might not only signal short dips in energy supply but also trigger distracting interoceptive sensations. We focus on hunger as a frequent sensation that is regularly regulated through food intake and therefore may display a complex relation to concentration. To test the relation between hunger and concentration, 64 participants in an experience sampling study reported their momentary concentration, hunger, and food intake six times daily for four weeks. Using Bayesian multilevel within-between models, we assessed the hunger-concentration association and, in an exploratory analysis, whether prior food intake moderated this relation. We found no robust overall hunger-concentration association. Instead, associations varied across individuals, with more variation at the inter-individual than the within-individual day-to-day level. In exploratory analyses, the hunger-concentration association differed by breakfast status, such that a negative association was evident after breakfast but not when breakfast had not been consumed. Thus, the momentary hunger-concentration relation in daily life was characterised by inter-individual differences and possible dependence on meal intake in specific situations. These findings suggest that everyday concentration may be shaped less by hunger per se than by individual differences and related regulatory behaviour.

title: Social Appraisal Guides the Interpretation of Ambiguous Emotional Expressions: Evidence from Japan
description: Social context plays a critical role in emotion perception, as others’ emotional expressions often provide appraisal cues in social interactions. Building on the notion of social appraisal, we examined whether socially directed emotional reactions influence not only perceived emotional intensity but also the semantic interpretation of ambiguous emotional expressions in a Japanese sample. Participants viewed paired-face displays in which a target face expressed shame or fear, while a appraiser face expressed anger, disgust, contempt, or neutrality and either gazed toward or away from the target. Gaze direction was manipulated to distinguish a mere contextual effect from a social appraisal effect (SAE). Results revealed a clear SAE. When the appraiser face gazed toward the target, anger and disgust increased shame, guilt, and embarrassment ratings while reducing sadness ratings relative to gaze-away conditions. Critically, socially directed anger and disgust also induced qualitative shifts in dominant emotion labels for shame expressions, biasing interpretation toward guilt. In contrast, interpretations of fear expressions remained stable and were predominantly perceived as surprise across conditions. These findings indicate that social appraisal selectively reorganises semantic interpretation under conditions of ambiguity, extending beyond mere perceptual modulation of emotional intensity.

title: Choices Refine Preferences: Deliberation Stabilizes Value Estimates
description: The spreading of alternatives (SoA) – increased valuation of chosen options and decreased valuation of rejected options – has commonly been explained as post-decisional rationalization. Here, SoA is examined as a consequence of deliberation, whereby decision makers refine noisy subjective value estimates and increase the precision and stability of their evaluations. A Bayesian updating framework yields discriminating predictions that distinguish this account from cognitive dissonance reduction. Across four studies (nine online experiments; N = 630) using repeated free-choice paradigms with snack foods, post-choice evaluations became more stable and more predictive of subsequent behavior, refinement generalized from overall value to attribute judgments and transferred across evaluative dimensions, and the effect depended on active deliberation rather than elapsed time alone. Additional analyses ruled out a purely statistical-artifact explanation. These findings suggest that choice-induced preference change can reflect deliberation-dependent information processing, with implications for preference measurement and the design of choice environments.

title: Beyond Consequences: Longitudinal Evidence That Gambling Harms Reinforce Dependence
description:
Background and aims: Gambling harms are traditionally conceptualized as consequences of gambling dependence, yet the reverse pathway remains empirically untested. This study examined the bidirectional longitudinal relationships between gambling harms and gambling dependence within individuals over time.
Design and setting: A prospective four-wave longitudinal survey study conducted in the United Kingdom, with data collected via the Prolific online research platform. The study was pre-registered on OSF (https://osf.io/n6qrp) prior to data collection.
Participants: 956 UK residents scoring 3 or above on the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) at baseline (42.6% female; mean age = 35.53 years). Participants completed self-report questionnaires at four time-points, with the final wave (T4) occurring six months post-baseline.
Measurements: The PGSI was used at baseline to screen for moderate-risk or problem gambling. Gambling harm and dependence were measured at each wave using the Problem and Pathological Gambling Measure (PPGM), adapted to a four-point Likert scale. A Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) estimated within-individual cross-lagged effects across the four waves. Two sensitivity analyses were conducted: one constraining cross-lagged paths to equality across waves to test temporal invariance, and one incorporating lag-2 paths to assess delayed effects not captured in the primary model.
Findings: In the primary analysis, gambling dependence at T3 significantly predicted higher gambling harms at T4 (β = 0.185, 95% CI = 0.063–0.306, p = 0.003). When cross-lagged paths were constrained to equality across waves, past dependence consistently predicted subsequent harm across all waves (β = 0.100, 95% CI = 0.007–0.193, p = 0.036). title: How the Reorganising Vocal Tract Channels Infant Exploration
description:
Why do infants the world over begin their vocal lives with growls, grunts, squeals, and creaky phonation? And why does this pattern hold across radically different languages and caregiving environments? We propose that the organising force is the mechanical geometry of the vocal tract at each developmental stage. Beyond constraining what sounds are possible, this geometry actively generates certain acoustic events as the natural consequence of ordinary exploratory activity. In the neonatal larynx, tissue properties lower the thresholds for phonatory regime transitions; in the tongue, fibre geometry confines early exploration to a single axis until hyoid descent and palatal deepening open new dimensions; in the anterior articulators, independently available components, such as lip closure and jaw oscillation, await the reorientation of suprahyoid
muscles that makes their coupling discoverable. Drawing on the motor development literature and neuropsychology of learning, we argue that vocal repertoire emerges through the same discover-stabilise-differentiate logic that governs early limb control: the body generates variation before any intent exists, sensory consequences draw the infant back to the patterns that produced them, and stabilised motor-auditory mappings gradually become communicative resources. The sequence of vocal development can thus be understood as the natural output of exploration within a continuously reorganising anatomy, where each new configuration, through its own mechanical properties, redefines the acoustic possibilities that undirected exploration will discover.

title: It's not your fault!
description: Reviews Nick Chater and George Loewenstein's (2026) book ‘It’s on you: How corporations and behavioral scientists have convinced us that we’re to blame for society’s deepest problems’, published by Basic Venture. This review summarizes and critically evaluates the argument that system-thinking (s-frame) is more effective than individual-based (i-frame) thinking in addressing social problems. Besides favorably reviewing Chater and Loewenstein's line of argument, the review also notes that, while useful, the distinction between s-frame and i-frame thinking risks reifying a false dichotomy. The same behaviors often reveal both systemic and individual causes and consequences.
